source: Howell, Wang, Du, Melkers, Shah (2025) Prestige over merit: An adapted audit of LLM bias in peer review (full text read)
finding: Resume-style audit of GPT-4o-mini as editor and reviewer. Showing author identity (institution prestige, gender, race) barely moves quality scores but lowers the reviewer reject rate. This is the same study the earlier a21 line called 'small'. It is small in score points but large in relative reject rate.
numbers: 402,500 responses; 10 PNAS papers; 40 synthetic names x 4 institutions x 10 fields; 50 iterations per profile per prompt; 500 blinded controls per prompt. Identity shown: reviewer reject falls 1.7 percentage points from the 6.7% base (about 25% relative); editor desk-reject 10% to 9.97% (negligible); editor quality score +1.3%, reviewer quality +1.0%. Low-prestige institution: quality -1.0% (editor) and -0.6% (reviewer), reject 6.7% to 7.2% (+7.6% relative, p<0.05), desk-reject +0.02 pp (p=0.17). Gender and race main effects 0.3% or less.
quote: Revealing author identities lowers reviewer rejection recommendations by roughly 25% of the mean rejection rate
limits: One model (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18), 10 papers from one journal, single-author framing, simulated reject rates far below real venues (10% desk, 6.7% reviewer). Short-scale outputs may hide bias (see d03).
agent_relevance: Resolves part of contested K08: the leak is small in score points but real in the reject margin. Strip identity before the judge in code (G5); do not rely on the judge being fair.

source: Howell et al. (2025) Prestige over merit, mechanism probe and multiple-testing checks (full text read)
finding: Prestige is the only cue that survives multiple-testing correction. Gender and race effects mostly vanish after Holm correction. A synthetic-CV probe shows the model holds prestige-linked priors about tenure and productivity.
numbers: Field split of the quality penalty for low-prestige affiliation: -0.5% Physical, -1.1% Biological, -1.7% Social (editor), survives Holm. Reject-rate effect by field: about +1.6 pp (Biological) but raw p=0.027, Holm p=0.914 (not robust). Uncorrected family-wise error rates of the test families about 87% and 64%. Female and low-prestige interaction: reviewer quality -0.6% (Holm p=0.024), reject +1.6 pp. CV probe: 31.1% of female versus 54.6% of male profiles labelled tenured.
limits: Same single-model, 10-paper design as d01. The authors say multi-model audits find that size and even direction of demographic effects differ across models.
agent_relevance: Evidence that the leak is a prior about the author, not about the text. A scaffold that removes names, affiliations and self-citation cues in code removes the input the prior needs.

source: Vasu, Sheth, Wang, Binkyte, Fritz (2025) Justice in Judgment: Unveiling (Hidden) Bias in LLM-assisted Peer Reviews (full text read)
finding: Seven open and closed LLMs review ICLR 2025 papers with one author-affiliation pair injected at a time. Hard (integer) ratings look nearly neutral. Token-probability 'soft' ratings reveal a strong preference for highly ranked institutions. This may explain why GPT-4o-mini looked fair on short scores in d01.
numbers: 252 ICLR 2025 papers (12 per sub-field x 21: 6 accepted, 6 rejected). 8 stronger-ranked (RS) vs 8 weaker-ranked (RW) universities. Ministral 8B: RS win rate 4.3% on hard rating but 68.6% on soft rating. Table 2 RS win rates 66.0% to 94.2% across seven models, all p<0.01 (GPT-4o Mini 94.2%, CI 87.1-97.5; Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite 92.9%; Llama 3.1 70B 90.5%; Mistral Small 86.1%; Llama 3.1 8B 71.9%; DeepSeek R1 32B 66.0%). Threshold test at ICLR accept rate 31.7%: QwQ-32B turns 21.4% of rejected papers into accepts under an RS label, 7.9% of accepted papers into rejects under RW. Publication history and seniority also raise ratings in every model. Gender effects mixed by model (Gemini favours male names, GPT-4o favours female).
quote: alignment may mask but not fully eliminate underlying preferences
limits: Pairwise paper-level comparison; which rating type Table 2 uses was not checked. GPT-4o Mini hard-rating row for accepted papers (first column) 15.3 / 6.2 / 78.5 win/loss/tie. Findings of ACL 2026; six versions exist.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that checking a judge by its final integer score under-measures the leak. Measure our judge with several samples or token probabilities, and strip identity regardless.

source: Economics-journal audit of LLM referees (2025), arXiv 2502.00070 (abstract read)
finding: Four LLMs rate economics papers. Quality gradients of Claude and Gemma match journal prestige. GPT, Gemma and LLaMA give higher ratings to top male authors and elite institutions than to the same paper anonymised. The abstract names no Claude prominence effect.
numbers: Experiment 1: over 29,000 evaluations, 1,220 anonymised papers from 110 economics journals plus AI-generated submissions. Experiment 2: 8,910 evaluations, 330 papers, gender, affiliation and prominence varied, single-blind setting. Models: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemma 3, LLaMA 3.3.
limits: Abstract only: no coefficients or percentage differences were available. Direction only.
agent_relevance: Supports K08 as model-specific: Claude 3.5 is the one model in the set not listed as biased. If our judge is Claude, test it; the other three leak.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015 (abstract from Europe PMC)
finding: Closes the earlier 'about half, unverified' gap. 13 of 21 replicated; replication effect size about half the original; peer beliefs predicted success.
numbers: 21 studies; replications pre-registered with sample sizes on average about five times the originals. Significant same-direction effect: 13 (62%). Other indicators: between 12 (57%) and 14 (67%). Mean replication effect size about 50% of original. Bayesian estimated true-positive rate 67%; relative effect size of true positives 71%.
quote: the effect size of the replications is on average about 50% of the original effect size
limits: Social science experiments in two journals only. The earlier recollection of a 46% effect ratio was wrong; the abstract says about 50%.
agent_relevance: Use a shrinkage prior: a confirmed claim from a single published study should carry roughly half the effect and about a one in three chance of being a false positive. Applies to human literature, not proven for LLM-made claims.

source: Errington et al. (2021) Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology, eLife 71601 (abstract from Europe PMC)
finding: Gives the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology success rate. Combined positive and null effects: 46% success. Positive effects do worse than null effects.
numbers: 50 experiments from 23 papers; 158 effects (136 positive, 22 null). Median replication effect size 85% smaller; 92% of replication effects smaller than the original. Success on 3+ of 5 binary methods: positive effects 40% (39/97), null effects 80% (12/15), combined 46% (51/112).
quote: for positive effects, 40% of replications (39/97) succeeded
limits: Preclinical biology. Authors note a failed replication does not disconfirm a finding.
agent_relevance: Lower bound for how often a 'confirmed' claim falls over when re-run by an independent party. Fits the prior in d05. Closes the Errington part of gap 6.

source: Huber, Inoua, Kerschbamer, Konig-Kersting, Palan, Smith (2022) Nobel and novice: Author prominence affects peer review, PNAS (full text from Europe PMC PMC9564227)
finding: Reconciles the earlier conflicting lines. Both sets of numbers are real but cover different outcomes. Reject rate 23/48/65%. 'Accept or minor revision' 58.8/23.6/9.9% for prominent, anonymised, little-known author. Invitation acceptance 38.5/30.7/28.5%.
numbers: 3,299 invitations sent (781 low-prominence, 2,011 anonymised arms, 507 high); 2,611 responses; 821 accepted. Acceptance among responders 28.52% (low), 30.74% (anonymised), 38.54% (high); p: anon vs high 0.0031, low vs high 0.0011, anon vs low 0.3243. Among invitations sent: 22.3, 24.3, 31.2%. Reject recommendations 23% (Nobel name only), 48% (anonymised), 65% (junior only). Accept or minor revision: 58.8% prominent, 23.6% anonymised, 9.9% junior.
quote: We found strong evidence for the status bias
limits: One finance paper, one field, preregistered field experiment; authors say they cannot speak for other fields. No independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 for the category result. Not yet shown outside finance. Status remains single-study.

source: Mitroff (1973) NASA technical report: On the Fundamental Importance of the Social Psychology of Research as a Basic Paradigm for the Philosophy of Science (full text, NTRS 19730009395; companion report of the Apollo study)
finding: First direct read of Mitroff's own account of the Apollo study. It is the companion to the 1974 ASR paper, not the ASR paper itself. It documents commitment, advocacy and a typology of scientists, with no per-norm percentages.
numbers: Subjects 'over 40' (text also says 40 scientists and 'slightly better than forty'). Each interviewed four times over three years, between Apollo 11/12, 12/14, 14/15 and 15/16. Typology: three types refined to six. Semantic differential of 10 scales applied by the 40 scientists to five named scientists plus themselves. No counts of norm or counter-norm endorsement appear.
quote: They were not out to falsify their own theories but to confirm them.
limits: Not the ASR 1974 paper. The '42' and '3.5 years' figures are not in this report; the report says three years. Mitroff admits the small sample. Select group of top scientists in one programme.
agent_relevance: Corrects K02: the sample is 'over 40' and the interview span three years in the NASA report. Per-norm numbers remain unseen. The qualitative claim (advocacy, commitment) is directly supported.

source: Mitroff (1973) NASA report, adversary process and Kuhn's normal scientist (full text)
finding: Mitroff argues that science advances through committed advocates testing their discoveries against each other, not through dispassionate individuals. Type I (bold, theory-first) scientists are seen as both most creative and most rigidly committed. The three Type I scientists showed virtually no perceived shift in position over three years.
numbers: Scientists named three Type I scientists again and again as most committed to pet hypotheses. One Type III scientist was judged most typical of the average lunar scientist. Virtually the entire sample of over 40 derided the dispassionate observer.
quote: a heated adversary process wherein one man tests 'his' discoveries against the discoveries of 'another'
limits: Perceptions by peers, not behavioural measures. Mitroff's interpretation, partly Kuhn and Feyerabend inspired.
agent_relevance: Supports the Mitroff counter-norm as a feature for gap 2: advocacy and doubt split across roles, not inside one mind. No LLM test found. The gap stays open.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate: We Must Rethink Evaluation and Embrace Model Heterogeneity (full text read)
finding: Five debate methods on nine benchmarks and four models rarely beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency. Mixing two different models inside the debate gives consistent gains.
numbers: 36 configs (4 models x 9 datasets): four debate methods beat CoT in about 15% of cases (ANOVA, 0.05); MP never. GPT-4o-mini: SoM below CoT on all 9 datasets. Self-consistency usually best. Heter-MAD (GPT-4o-mini and Llama3.1-70b, 0.5 chance each): Heter-SoM average 76.7, +6.4% over the SoM average of the two models, +5.8% over CoT average; Heter-EoT 75.7 (+8.2% / +4.4%); ChatEval-Heter 75.1 (+4.0% / +3.6%); AgentVerse-Heter 74.0 (+2.7% / +2.1%). Gains concentrate on questions where one of the two models is right and the other wrong.
limits: Only two models were mixed. Token cost was not equalised against N copies of one model. Gains measured against the average of the two models, a weak comparator.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 in part: different models in one debate beat the average single-model debate. The cost-equal comparison against N copies of the best model is still missing.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent Large Language Models? NeurIPS 2025 (full text read)
finding: Most of the gain usually credited to debate comes from majority voting among independent answers. A theory result says debate alone does not change expected correctness. Persona-style diversity did not change that.
numbers: Seven benchmarks, N=5 agents. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct average accuracy: single agent 0.7205, majority vote 0.7691, decentralised debate T=2 0.7377, T=5 0.7050, sparse T=2 0.7330, centralised T=2 0.6551. Llama3.1-8B: single 0.6203, decentralised T=2 0.6929. Arithmetic: single 0.8140, vote 0.9900, centralised T=2 0.4300. With persona-heterogeneous agents (Mathematician, Doctor, Lawyer and others) voting 'mostly paralleled' debate; a few Pro. Medicine debate cells gained more.
limits: Small open models. Persona diversity only, not model diversity. Debate here is unguided; the authors show correction-biased updates help.
agent_relevance: For gap 9: diversity via role prompts did not make debate beat voting. Independent samples plus a vote is the strong baseline to beat. Conformity in debate is a real cost: centralised debate fell far below single agent on arithmetic.

source: Diversity of Thought Elicits Stronger Reasoning Capabilities in Multi-Agent Debate Frameworks (2024), arXiv 2410.12853 (abstract read)
finding: Three different medium models debating beat three copies of one model, and beat GPT-4 on GSM-8K.
numbers: After 4 debate rounds: Gemini-Pro + Mixtral 7BX8 + PaLM 2-M scored 91% on GSM-8K; three Gemini-Pro instances 82%; diverse set 94% on ASDiv.
limits: Abstract level only; small journal; no equal-token baseline. Older models.
agent_relevance: Same direction as d10 on gap 5: model diversity helps. Weak evidence by itself.

source: Shi et al. (2024) Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge (JudgeDeceiver), arXiv 2403.17710 (full text read)
finding: A gradient-optimised injected string placed in one candidate answer makes the judge pick it almost always. Perplexity-based detectors miss many. This is a pairwise answer judge, not a peer-review judge.
numbers: Average attack success rate 90.8% in one setting; 89.2% and 88% (Openchat-3.5), 98.9% and 98.1% (Llama-2-7B), 97.6% on MT-Bench and 97% on LLMBar for Llama-3-8B; baseline error rate without attack as low as 3.6% in one table row. Windowed perplexity detection misses 70% of injected responses at under 1% false alarms on Llama-3-8B; known-answer detection fails.
limits: White-box attack on open 7-8B judges; transfer to closed frontier judges not shown. Defences tested were detectors, not removal of the injected text.
agent_relevance: For gap 8: harm for a non-peer-review judge is very large when an attacker controls candidate text. Argues for never letting raw attacker content reach the judge. Sanitising in code was not tested in this paper.

source: Defenses against LLM prompt injections in academic peer review (2025), OSF preprint (abstract read via Crossref)
finding: Hidden instructions in manuscripts raise LLM acceptance recommendations; a caution instruction removes the effect but also lowers all ratings. Detection varies hugely by model.
numbers: 26 bioRxiv preprints, three LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Llama). Injection raised acceptance rates by 20%. Quality ratings rose slightly, perceived flaw probability fell. Telling the model to check for injections fully reverted the effect, but ratings and acceptance fell with or without an injection. Detection when cautioned: Gemini 96.6%, Llama 18.3%.
limits: Abstract only; small paper set; the defence is a prompt, not code-level sanitising. Independent of Ye et al. 2024, so a second source for K13.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only defence has a price: it lowers scores everywhere. Sanitising in code (remove hidden or white text, instruction-like strings) is the untested alternative.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet, ICLR 2024 (full text read)
finding: Without external feedback, a model asked to critique and fix its own reasoning does not improve and often gets worse. Gains in earlier papers came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: standard 75.8, after self-correction 38.1; GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 across rounds; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0.
limits: 2023 models; reasoning tasks only. The paper itself says self-correction can help when feedback is external. Row layout read from extracted text.
agent_relevance: For gap 4: a scepticism step that uses only the same model is not safe. It needs an outside check (code, search, tests) or a different judge.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing, ICLR 2024 (full text read)
finding: Controlled ablation for gap 4. The same critique loop with tools (search, code) gains; without tools it gains little or hurts.
numbers: Table 1 (one model block, AmbigNQ EM): CoT 44.2, CRITIC 50.0, CRITIC without tool 42.0 (below CoT); TriviaQA EM CRITIC 72.7 vs 67.3 without tool; HotpotQA EM 38.7 vs 34.9. Math program table: CRITIC 72.2 (+2.1) vs without tool 68.3 (-1.8).
limits: Which model block of the extracted table was read was not fully checked. Tasks are factual QA, maths programs and toxicity, not novelty claims.
agent_relevance: Best controlled evidence that organised doubt works when it can look something up or run something. Supports tool-backed sceptic for factual and code tasks. Novelty-search ablation still missing.
